13 Second-Order Linear Homogeneous Equations, Auxiliary Roots & Wronskian Theory Standard [1 mark]
Consider the second-order linear homogeneous differential equation y′′−2y′+y=0y'' - 2y' + y = 0y′′−2y′+y=0. \\
If one of the fundamental solutions is y1(x)=exy_1(x) = e^xy1​(x)=ex, and the Wronskian of two linearly independent solutions y1(x)y_1(x)y1​(x) and y2(x)y_2(x)y2​(x) is given by W(y1,y2)(x)=5e2xW(y_1, y_2)(x) = 5e^{2x}W(y1​,y2​)(x)=5e2x, find the unknown parameter kkk in y2(x)=kxexy_2(x) = kxe^xy2​(x)=kxex.
A. k=−1k = -1k=−1
B. k=−5k = -5k=−5
C. k=1k = 1k=1
D. k=5k = 5k=5 ✓
Correct Answer: (D) — k=5k = 5k=5
The given differential equation is y′′−2y′+y=0y'' - 2y' + y = 0y′′−2y′+y=0. The characteristic equation is r2−2r+1=0r^2 - 2r + 1 = 0r2−2r+1=0, which factors as (r−1)2=0(r-1)^2 = 0(r−1)2=0. Thus, the roots are repeated: r1=r2=1r_1 = r_2 = 1r1​=r2​=1. \\
One fundamental solution is given as y1(x)=exy_1(x) = e^xy1​(x)=ex. For a second-order linear homogeneous equation y′′+p(x)y′+q(x)y=0y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0y′′+p(x)y′+q(x)y=0 with a known solution y1(x)y_1(x)y1​(x), the Wronskian is given by W(y1,y2)(x)=y1(x)y2′(x)−y1′(x)y2(x)=Ce−∫p(x)dxW(y_1, y_2)(x) = y_1(x)y_2'(x) - y_1'(x)y_2(x) = C e^{-\int p(x) dx}W(y1​,y2​)(x)=y1​(x)y2′​(x)−y1′​(x)y2​(x)=Ce−∫p(x)dx. \\
In our equation, p(x)=−2p(x) = -2p(x)=−2. So, −∫p(x)dx=−∫(−2)dx=2x-\int p(x) dx = -\int (-2) dx = 2x−∫p(x)dx=−∫(−2)dx=2x. Therefore, W(y1,y2)(x)=Ce2xW(y_1, y_2)(x) = C e^{2x}W(y1​,y2​)(x)=Ce2x. \\
We are given that W(y1,y2)(x)=5e2xW(y_1, y_2)(x) = 5e^{2x}W(y1​,y2​)(x)=5e2x, which means C=5C = 5C=5. \\
We are also given y1(x)=exy_1(x) = e^xy1​(x)=ex and y2(x)=kxexy_2(x) = kxe^xy2​(x)=kxex. \\
Let's compute the Wronskian using these forms: \\
y1′(x)=exy_1'(x) = e^xy1′​(x)=ex \\
y2′(x)=ddx(kxex)=k(1⋅ex+x⋅ex)=kex(1+x)y_2'(x) = \frac{d}{dx}(kxe^x) = k(1 \cdot e^x + x \cdot e^x) = ke^x(1+x)y2′​(x)=dxd​(kxex)=k(1⋅ex+x⋅ex)=kex(1+x)
\\
Now, substitute into the Wronskian formula: \\
W(y1,y2)(x)=y1(x)y2′(x)−y1′(x)y2(x)W(y_1, y_2)(x) = y_1(x)y_2'(x) - y_1'(x)y_2(x)W(y1​,y2​)(x)=y1​(x)y2′​(x)−y1′​(x)y2​(x)
W(y1,y2)(x)=ex⋅[kex(1+x)]−ex⋅[kxex]W(y_1, y_2)(x) = e^x \cdot [ke^x(1+x)] - e^x \cdot [kxe^x]W(y1​,y2​)(x)=ex⋅[kex(1+x)]−ex⋅[kxex]
W(y1,y2)(x)=ke2x(1+x)−kxe2xW(y_1, y_2)(x) = ke^{2x}(1+x) - kxe^{2x}W(y1​,y2​)(x)=ke2x(1+x)−kxe2x
W(y1,y2)(x)=ke2x+kxe2x−kxe2xW(y_1, y_2)(x) = ke^{2x} + kxe^{2x} - kxe^{2x}W(y1​,y2​)(x)=ke2x+kxe2x−kxe2x
W(y1,y2)(x)=ke2xW(y_1, y_2)(x) = ke^{2x}W(y1​,y2​)(x)=ke2x
\\
We equate this to the given Wronskian: \\
ke2x=5e2xke^{2x} = 5e^{2x}ke2x=5e2x
\\
Therefore, k=5k = 5k=5.
